Weekend Project Update: Expanding My Self-Hosted Media Server with Jellyfin, FlareSolverr, and Profilarr

Renato
7 min read
·
Jan 23, 2026

A few months ago, I built my own media server. Not just any media server — a fully automated setup that downloads, organizes, and streams content just like the big streaming services do, but completely under my control.

Since then, I’ve made some significant improvements. This is the story of how I evolved .

The Original Vision: My Own Streaming Service

The initial goal was simple:

  • Automatically download TV shows and movies
  • Organize everything properly with artwork and metadata
  • Stream to any device in my house (or anywhere via Tailscale)
  • Never manually rename or move files again
  • Have new episodes of my favorite shows appear automatically

Basically, I wanted my own personal Netflix that actually has everything I want to watch.

The Evolved Stack: More Than Just *Arr

After running the original setup for a while, I identified pain points and opportunities for improvement. Here’s what the stack looks like now:

Core Streaming:

  • Plex: The primary streaming interface — think Netflix, but for your own content. Mainly used on my TV.
  • Jellyfin: The open-source alternative — no Plex Pass required, completely free, and increasingly powerful. Used everywhere else.

Automation Layer:

  • Sonarr: Automated TV show management
  • Radarr: Automated movie management
  • qBittorrent: The download client
  • Prowlarr: The indexer manager that finds content across multiple sources

The New Additions:

  • FlareSolverr: Bypasses Cloudflare protection on torrent indexers
  • Profilarr: Manages quality profiles across all *Arr apps from one place

Infrastructure:

  • Caddy: Reverse proxy for clean URLs and SSL certificates (referenced via external network)
  • Tailscale: Secure remote access without exposing ports (from my previous setup)

The beauty of this expanded setup is that it’s still all containerized with Docker, now leveraging a shared Caddy network for seamless reverse proxy integration.

Phase 0: Understanding How This Actually Works

Before diving into the updates, let me refresh the workflow magic:

  1. I tell Sonarr “I want to watch Breaking Bad”
  2. Sonarr searches torrent indexers via Prowlarr to find available episodes
  3. FlareSolverr helps bypass Cloudflare-protected sites (new addition!)
  4. Sonarr sends the best quality torrent to qBittorrent
  5. qBittorrent downloads the files
  6. Sonarr automatically moves and renames them to a clean structure
  7. Both Plex AND Jellyfin scan the folder and add the show with artwork and metadata
  8. I open either Plex or Jellyfin on my TV (or any other device) and hit play

For ongoing shows, Sonarr monitors release schedules and automatically downloads new episodes when they air. No manual work required.

Phase 1: The Enhanced Docker Compose Setup

Here’s the complete configuration that now powers everything:

services:
  jellyfin:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/jellyfin:latest
    container_name: jellyfin
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=10
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
    volumes:
      - ./jellyfin/library:/config
      - ./media/tv:/data/tv
      - ./media/movies:/data/movies
    ports:
      - 8096:8096/tcp
      - 7359:7359/udp
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
  plex:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/plex:latest
    container_name: plex
    network_mode: host
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=10
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
      - VERSION=docker
      - PLEX_CLAIM=claim-yourclaimtoken
    volumes:
      - ./plex/config:/config
      - ./media/tv:/tv
      - ./media/movies:/movies
    restart: unless-stopped
  sonarr:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/sonarr:latest
    container_name: sonarr
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=10
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
    volumes:
      - ./sonarr/config:/config
      - ./media/tv:/tv
      - ./downloads:/downloads
    ports:
      - 8989:8989
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
  radarr:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/radarr:latest
    container_name: radarr
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=10
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
    volumes:
      - ./radarr/config:/config
      - ./media/movies:/movies
      - ./downloads:/downloads
    ports:
      - 7878:7878
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
  qbittorrent:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/qbittorrent:latest
    container_name: qbittorrent
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=10
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
      - WEBUI_PORT=8081
      - TORRENTING_PORT=6881
    volumes:
      - ./qbittorrent/config:/config
      - ./downloads:/downloads
    ports:
      - 8081:8081
      - 6881:6881
      - 6881:6881/udp
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
  prowlarr:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/prowlarr:latest
    container_name: prowlarr
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=10
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
    volumes:
      - ./prowlarr/config:/config
    ports:
      - 9696:9696
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
  flaresolverr:
    image: ghcr.io/flaresolverr/flaresolverr:latest
    container_name: flaresolverr
    environment:
      - LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-info}
      - LOG_HTML=${LOG_HTML:-false}
      - CAPTCHA_SOLVER=${CAPTCHA_SOLVER:-none}
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
    volumes:
      - ./flaresolverr/config:/config
    ports:
      - 8191:8191
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
  profilarr:
    image: santiagosayshey/profilarr:latest
    container_name: profilarr
    environment:
      - TZ=Your/Timezone
    volumes:
      - ./profilarr/config:/config
    ports:
      - 6868:6868
    networks:
      - caddy_default
    restart: unless-stopped
networks:
  caddy_default:
    external: true

Critical Settings and Key Changes:

Network Architecture:

  • All services now connect to caddy_default external network (except Plex which uses host mode)
  • This integrates seamlessly with my existing Caddy reverse proxy setup
  • Clean URLs like sonarr.yourdomain.com instead of 192.168.1.x:8989
  • Automatic SSL certificates via Caddy

Permission Management:

  • PUID=1000 and PGID=10 ensure containers have proper file permissions
  • You can find your user’s PUID/PGID by running id $USER in terminal
  • Critical for avoiding “permission denied” errors when moving files

Volume Mapping Consistency:

  • All services share /downloads for the handoff to work
  • Jellyfin uses /data/tv and /data/movies (different path structure than Plex)
  • Both point to the same underlying ./media directory

Understanding the Directory Structure:

./media/tv          → TV shows live here (final destination)
./media/movies      → Movies live here (final destination)
./downloads         → Temporary download location (shared between all services)
./jellyfin/library  → Jellyfin configuration and metadata
./plex/config       → Plex configuration and metadata

The key insight: when a download completes, Sonarr/Radarr move files from /downloads to the appropriate media folder and rename them. Both Plex and Jellyfin then scan the same media folders but maintain separate configurations and metadata.

Directory Setup:

mkdir -p media/{tv,movies} downloads
mkdir -p jellyfin/library plex/config sonarr/config radarr/config
mkdir -p qbittorrent/config prowlarr/config flaresolverr/config profilarr/config
docker-compose up -d

Phase 2: Why I Added Jellyfin (The Plex Alternative)

This was the biggest change to my setup. Why run both Plex and Jellyfin?

The Plex Problem:

  • Plex Pass subscription for premium features
  • Remote play is now paid option
  • Proprietary software with potential future rug-pulls

The Jellyfin Advantage:

  • Completely free and open-source
  • Hardware transcoding included out of the box
  • More customization options
  • Growing community and plugin ecosystem
  • No telemetry or tracking

Phase 3: FlareSolverr (The Cloudflare Bypass)

This was a game-changer for indexer reliability.

The Problem: Many torrent indexers hide behind Cloudflare protection to prevent scraping and DDoS attacks. When Prowlarr tries to search these sites, it gets blocked by Cloudflare’s “Checking your browser” page.

The Solution: FlareSolverr acts as a proxy that can bypass Cloudflare protection by simulating a real browser. It handles the JavaScript challenges and CAPTCHA solving, then passes the actual content back to Prowlarr.

Configuration in Prowlarr:

  1. Settings → Indexers → Add FlareSolverr
  2. Tags: Create a tag like “flaresolverr”
  3. Host: http://flaresolverr:8191
  4. Test and save

Then for any indexer that’s Cloudflare-protected:

  1. Edit the indexer
  2. Add the “flaresolverr” tag
  3. Save

Prowlarr will now route requests for that indexer through FlareSolverr automatically. Success rate went from 60% to 95% on protected sites.

Phase 4: Profilarr (Quality Profile Management)

In the original setup, I maintained separate quality profiles in Sonarr and Radarr. Want 1080p for most content but 4K for specific shows? You’d configure it twice. Want to adjust preferred words or release group rankings? Update both apps.

This gets tedious fast, especially when you’re fine-tuning what quality you want and which release groups you prefer.

What Profilarr Does:

Profilarr provides a single interface to manage quality profiles across all your *Arr applications. Create a profile once, and it syncs to Sonarr, Radarr, and any other compatible apps.

My Setup:

  • 4K Profile: For specific shows/movies I really care about
  • 1080p WEB-DL Profile: For most TV shows — high quality, smaller files
  • 1080p Bluray Profile: For movies — better quality than WEB-DL
  • 720p Profile: For older shows or things I don’t care about as much

Configuration:

  1. Access Profilarr at http://profilarr:6868
  2. Add Sonarr and Radarr connections with API keys
  3. Create profiles with preferred codecs, release groups, and quality cutoffs
  4. Push to all apps with one click

The result: consistent quality across my entire library without duplicating configuration work.

Phase 5: The Caddy Integration (Clean URLs)

Since all services (except Plex) are on the caddy_default network, I have them accessible via reverse proxy with SSL:

sonarr.mydomain.com {
    reverse_proxy sonarr:8989
}
radarr.mydomain.com {
    reverse_proxy radarr:7878
}
jellyfin.mydomain.com {
    reverse_proxy jellyfin:8096
}
prowlarr.mydomain.com {
    reverse_proxy prowlarr:9696
}
profilarr.mydomain.com {
    reverse_proxy profilarr:6868
}
qbit.mydomain.com {
    reverse_proxy qbittorrent:8081
}

Combined with Tailscale, I can securely access my entire media stack from anywhere.

The Privacy Consideration (Still Being Real)

I again need to address the elephant in the room: torrenting copyrighted content is illegal in most places. This setup is technically designed for legitimate uses — downloading Linux ISOs, public domain content, or backing up media you own.

That said, I’m not going to pretend that’s what most people use this for. If you do choose to use this setup for less legitimate purposes, understand the risks:

  • Your ISP can see torrent traffic and may throttle or log it
  • Your real IP is visible to everyone in the torrent swarm (potentially thousands of peers)
  • Copyright trolls monitor popular torrents and collect IPs
  • You could receive DMCA notices, ISP warnings, or legal action

A VPN is essential if you’re torrenting anything remotely questionable. I use Mullvad (as mentioned in my previous privacy setup).

Final Thoughts

Building this expanded media server was one of the most rewarding self-hosting projects I’ve undertaken. The *Arr stack is mature, well-documented, and just works. Docker makes deployment trivial. Adding Jellyfin provides insurance against vendor lock-in. FlareSolverr solved indexer reliability issues. Profilarr simplified quality management.

And the end result? I now have TWO streaming services that are better than any paid subscription because they have exactly what I want, when I want it, how I want it.

The best part? Once it’s set up, it runs itself. New episodes appear like magic. Quality improves automatically. Both Plex and Jellyfin stay in sync. I haven’t touched the configuration in weeks. I just add shows or movies when I think of something I want to watch.

Is it legal? That depends on what you download.

Is it worth it? For me, absolutely. There’s something deeply satisfying about owning your infrastructure and having complete control over your media.

Would I recommend it? If you’re comfortable with Docker and have the time to learn the ecosystem, yes. The initial setup takes a weekend. The ongoing maintenance is minimal. The payoff is permanent.
